passage:
"Why are you still up?" Ira asked, finding her brother on the balcony at one in the morning, his phone glowing.
"Just typing something."
"To Mitali?"
"Only 'hope your exam went well'. That's harmless, right?"
"At one a.m.? What do you actually want her to do with it?"
Harsha stared at the half-written line. "Reply fast. Prove she still cares."
"And if she doesn't reply?"
"Then I check every ten minutes till morning." He laughed, but it came out thin.
"So it's not really about her exam."
"No." He deleted the words slowly. "If I still want to wish her something next week, I'll decide in daylight."
"Fair."
He pressed and held the chat, tapped mute, and handed Ira the phone. "Charge it in your room tonight?"
"Deal. Chai at seven, then."

qa.q: Where did Ira find Harsha at one in the morning?
qa.a: On the balcony, with his phone glowing.

qa.q: What did Harsha hope for when he typed the message to Mitali?
qa.a: He felt lonely and anxious to know whether Mitali still cared; he admits he wanted a fast reply as proof, and his thin laugh shows how uneasy the waiting made him.

qa.q: Which choice helped Harsha most, and why?
qa.a: Muting the chat and charging his phone in Ira's room took away the late-night temptation, and moving the decision to daylight let him choose about contact with a clear head.

qa.q: How might Mitali see a message like that arriving at one a.m.?
qa.a: She might feel confused or pressured, reading it as a test of her feelings rather than a simple wish about her exam.

grounding: Shows the urge to text an ex late at night and the wise choice to decide about contact consciously, mute the chat and let time pass.

passage:
For the first month after Nilesh and I ended things, I kept asking our friend Rukhsar small questions. Was he at the canteen? Did he look sad? I told myself I was just curious. Really, I was keeping watch on him through her, and every answer kept me awake longer.
One night I caught myself drafting a text to him at 2 a.m.: "Saw a song you'd like." I didn't send it. I asked myself a plain question instead: would I send this at noon? The answer was no.
So I muted his chat and archived our photos, not deleted, just out of sight. I told Rukhsar she didn't have to report on him anymore, and she looked relieved. Some nights I still reach for my phone. But the pull is weaker now, and I'm sleeping again. The weeks are doing slow, quiet work.
— Nirmala

qa.q: What text did Nirmala draft at 2 a.m.?
qa.a: "Saw a song you'd like."

qa.q: Why did Nirmala keep asking Rukhsar about Nilesh?
qa.a: Nirmala felt hurt and restless after the breakup and hoped for news of him, but each answer kept Nirmala awake longer, so the questions fed the pain instead of easing it.

qa.q: What small steps helped Nirmala stop keeping tabs?
qa.a: Asking "would I send this at noon?", muting Nilesh's chat, archiving the photos and telling Rukhsar she no longer had to report on him.

qa.q: What would change for Nilesh if Nirmala had sent the 2 a.m. text?
qa.a: He might feel pulled back into a finished relationship and unsure how to answer, and both of them would have to go through the ending again.

grounding: Illustrates the pull to keep tabs on an ex through a friend and a late-night text, and the wiser choice to mute contact and let time work.

passage:
The college library closed at eight, and Shankar and Binita still shelved returns together on Thursdays, as they had before the breakup. "See? We're good at being friends," Binita said, handing him a stack.
Shankar nodded. He had worn the shirt she once liked, and he knew why. Every time she laughed at his jokes, something in his chest lifted; every time she smiled at a message on her phone, it dropped.
At the returns trolley he stopped. "Can I be honest? I think I'm still hoping. These Thursdays feel good for an hour and bad for two days."
Binita put the books down. "I wondered."
"Could we take a break from the shifts for a couple of months? I'll ask the librarian to move me to Tuesdays. Not goodbye. Just some space before we try this again."
She nodded slowly. "Okay. Thank you for saying it."

qa.q: On which day did Shankar and Binita shelve returns together?
qa.a: On Thursdays.

qa.q: What do Shankar's reactions to Binita's laugh and her phone suggest about his feelings?
qa.a: He is still hoping to get back together: he feels lifted when she laughs and hurt when she smiles at someone else's message.

qa.q: What was wise about how Shankar handled the friendship?
qa.a: He admitted his hope honestly and asked for a couple of months apart by moving to Tuesdays, instead of staying close to keep a door open.

qa.q: How might Binita see Shankar's request?
qa.a: She had half expected it ("I wondered"), so she may feel sad but also relieved and grateful that he was honest rather than pretending.

grounding: Shows an attempt to stay friends while one person still hopes, and the wise move of naming it honestly and taking distance first.

passage:
Dear Sachin,
I've started this email four times, so I'll just say it.
When we ended things in March, we promised to stay friends, and I meant it. The late-night calls, Sunday chess at the park, the voice notes: I liked all of it. But last week, when you asked me to come to your cousin's wedding "as your plus-one, just for fun", I saw your face when I hesitated. I think you're still hoping, and I've let it continue because it was comfortable for me.
That isn't fair to you. So I want to ask honestly: are these calls helping you, or making it harder? For my part, I think we need a few months apart before we try friendship again. No chess, no calls, for now.
I'll miss you. That part is true too.
Suraj

qa.q: When did Suraj and Sachin end things?
qa.a: In March.

qa.q: How does Suraj feel about having kept the calls going?
qa.a: Suraj feels guilty, admitting it "isn't fair" and was comfortable for Suraj, and also sad about the loss, saying "I'll miss you."

qa.q: What would you advise Suraj to do after sending the email?
qa.a: Keep the promised break from calls and chess even if Sachin reaches out, and check honestly after a few months whether friendship feels possible.

qa.q: How might Sachin feel reading this email?
qa.a: Sachin may feel hurt and embarrassed that the hope was noticed, but also respected, because Suraj asked honestly instead of letting the plus-one question hang.

grounding: Illustrates trying friendship after a breakup while one person still hopes, and choosing to ask honestly and take distance first.

passage:
Three weeks after Vikas broke up with me by text, I was still replaying it in the shower, on the bus, in the middle of lectures. He'd said he "needed space", then was holding hands with someone at the fest two days later. I felt stupid and bitter.
One evening my hostel friends were complaining about exes, and I opened my mouth to tell them what Vikas had once confided about his father's drinking. Everyone would have gasped. For a second I wanted that.
I shut my mouth and went up to the terrace instead. I wrote everything I was angry about in my notebook, two full pages. The anger told me something true: I deserve honesty when things end. Keeping his secret didn't mean he was right. It meant I got to stay someone I respect. I haven't forgiven him. But the replaying is slowing down.
— Nazia

qa.q: How did Vikas break up with Nazia?
qa.a: By text.

qa.q: What was Nazia feeling when about to tell the hostel friends Vikas's secret?
qa.a: Bitter and hurt; for a second Nazia wanted the group's gasp, a wish to make Vikas look bad after feeling stupid over the breakup.

qa.q: What did Nazia do with the anger instead of spreading the secret?
qa.a: Nazia went to the terrace, wrote two pages in a notebook, and treated the anger as information: a sign of deserving honesty when things end.

qa.q: What would change for Vikas if Nazia had told the group about his father?
qa.a: A private family pain he shared in trust would become hostel gossip, hurting him and his family far beyond the breakup.

grounding: Shows replaying an ex's wrongs with bitterness, using anger as information, and refusing to spread the ex's private matters.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Tuesday
Vishal came in today because his mentor noticed him snapping at people in the lab. He talked for twenty minutes about Yamini: how she had cancelled their trip, how she had "used" him for notes, how she ended it the week before his exams. His jaw was tight, and he kept circling back to the same three events, as if telling them again might change them.
He admitted he had been hinting to their shared friends that Yamini "couldn't be trusted", and that two of them had stopped sitting with her. He looked uneasy saying it.
I told him the anger made sense; it was pointing at real hurt. We talked about the difference between feeling it and using it against her. By the end he said he would stop the hints and tell those two friends he'd been unfair. We agreed he would write his anger out before bed and come back next Tuesday.

qa.q: How long did Vishal talk about Yamini?
qa.a: For twenty minutes.

qa.q: What do Vishal's tight jaw and repeated story suggest?
qa.a: He is still bitter and angry; circling back to the same three events shows he feels stuck in the hurt.

qa.q: What plan did the counsellor help Vishal make?
qa.a: To stop the hints, tell the two friends he had been unfair, write his anger out before bed, and return next Tuesday.

qa.q: What is it like for Yamini when friends stop sitting with her?
qa.a: She may feel isolated and confused, cut off from friends because of a story told about her without her knowing.

grounding: Illustrates bitterness after a breakup turning into turning friends against the ex, and a counsellor helping the anger be felt rather than used.

passage:
The fourth unknown number that week rang while Tanuja was weighing rice at her father's shop in Kasba Sirsi. She knew the voice at once. "Just talk to me once," said Deepu.
"I said no in May. This is the last time: don't call me again." She hung up, hands shaking.
Her cousin Sharmila, stacking soap boxes, had heard. "He's been waiting near the bus stand too, hasn't he?"
Tanuja nodded, eyes down. "Maybe I was too friendly before."
"This is not on you. He's the one who won't stop." Sharmila helped her screenshot every message and number, with dates, into one folder. Then Tanuja blocked the new number.
That evening they told her father together. He listened, went quiet, then said, "Tomorrow morning we go to the women's help desk at the police station. You won't take the bus alone till this ends."

qa.q: Where was Tanuja when the fourth unknown number rang?
qa.a: Weighing rice at her father's shop in Kasba Sirsi.

qa.q: Why did Tanuja say "Maybe I was too friendly before"?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and scared and wrongly blamed herself for Deepu's behaviour, which shows in her lowered eyes and shaking hands.

qa.q: Which steps protected Tanuja?
qa.a: A clear final no, saved screenshots with dates, blocking the number, telling her father that evening, and a plan to visit the women's help desk.

qa.q: How does Tanuja's father see the situation?
qa.a: As a real safety problem: he takes it seriously, plans the police help desk visit for the next morning, and makes sure she won't travel alone.

grounding: Shows an ex who keeps calling after a no, and the wise steps of a final no, blocking, saving evidence and telling family and police.

Hiroshi found another paper bag hanging on his apartment door in Osaka: his favourite rice crackers and a note, "I'll wait as long as it takes." It was the ninth since he had told Mika, in April, that it was over.
He almost threw it away. Tariq, his flatmate, stopped him. "Photograph it first. With the note."
"It feels stupid. People will laugh. A guy scared of his ex."
"It isn't stupid. You said no. She keeps coming. That's the whole story."
They sat at the kitchen table and listed everything: each bag, each message from new accounts, the evening she waited outside his office. Hiroshi sent one last message: "Do not contact me again. I am blocking you and reporting this." Then he blocked her.
That evening Tariq walked with him to the local police box, the folder of photos in Hiroshi's hands. His shoulders dropped a little once the officer began writing.

qa.q: How many bags had Hiroshi received since April?
qa.a: This was the ninth since he told Mika in April that it was over.

qa.q: Why did Hiroshi almost throw the bag away?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and ashamed, afraid people would laugh at "a guy scared of his ex", so he wanted to hide it.

qa.q: What helped Hiroshi move from shame to action?
qa.a: Tariq's plain reassurance, a written list of every incident, one clear final message, blocking Mika, and reporting it at the police box that evening.

qa.q: How does Tariq see Mika's behaviour?
qa.a: As simple harassment: Hiroshi said no and she keeps coming, so there is nothing to be embarrassed about.

grounding: Illustrates being harassed by an ex after saying no, with a final no, blocking, evidence and a report, and the message that it is not the target's fault.

passage:
At 7:40 every morning Sachin checked three things before brushing his teeth: Nandini's profile, her friends' stories, and whether she showed as online. It had been five months since she ended it.
On Saturday he found himself on the metro towards Andheri, where her new office was. He hadn't decided to go; his feet had. Two stops before, he caught his reflection in the dark window, unshaved, gripping the phone like a lifeline, and got off at Marol.
On the platform bench he typed, "Bhaiya, can you talk?" His brother called within a minute.
"I was going to her office," Sachin said. "I don't even know why."
"Because it hurts, not because it's love," his brother said gently. "Come home. And on Monday we'll book the college counsellor."
Sachin sat there until the next train back, then removed her profile from his favourites.

qa.q: At what time did Sachin check Nandini's profile every morning?
qa.a: At 7:40, before brushing his teeth.

qa.q: What did Sachin feel when he saw his reflection in the metro window?
qa.a: He felt shaken and ashamed at how far the pain had taken him, seeing himself unshaved and gripping his phone like a lifeline, and got off at Marol.

qa.q: What steps did Sachin take instead of going to Nandini's office?
qa.a: He got off early, called his brother, agreed to book the college counsellor, and removed Nandini's profile from his favourites.

qa.q: How might Nandini feel if Sachin had appeared outside her office?
qa.a: She would likely feel frightened and watched, since she ended things five months ago and never asked to see him.

grounding: Shows being unable to stop watching an ex's life, nearly showing up, and turning instead to family and a counsellor for support.

"You made a second account?" Chetan held up Raghav's laptop. "Raghav, these are all Kritika's photos."
"It's just to see she's okay."
"She blocked you. That was her answer."

"Then it's not about her anymore. It's about how much this hurts."

passage:
Last winter, after Harish and I broke up, he posted a story with a blurred picture from a trip we'd taken, captioned "some memories are worth sharing". It showed nothing private, but I knew what else was on his phone. For four days I barely ate. I checked his profile every hour. I told nobody, because I felt foolish for having trusted him at all.
On the fifth day my Masi called and heard it in my voice. I told her everything, crying. She didn't lecture me. She said, "If he shares anything, that is his crime. Your only job now is to keep proof." That evening she sat with me while I saved his post and messages, and the next morning she came with me to the cyber cell to ask how to report.
Nothing was ever leaked. But I learned that carrying it alone was the heaviest part.
— Sarita

qa.q: What caption did Harish put on the story?
qa.a: "some memories are worth sharing"

qa.q: Why did Sarita tell nobody for four days?
qa.a: Sarita felt ashamed and foolish for trusting Harish, and was so frightened that eating became hard and checking his profile became hourly.

qa.q: What did Masi do that helped?
qa.a: She listened without lecturing, called any sharing Harish's crime, helped save the post and messages that evening, and went with Sarita to the cyber cell the next morning.

qa.q: What would have changed if Sarita had kept carrying it alone?
qa.a: The fear and hourly checking would likely have gone on, with no proof saved and no report made if Harish did leak something.

grounding: Illustrates fearing an ex will leak private material, the harm of bearing it alone, and the relief of keeping proof and going to the cyber cell with a trusted adult.

passage:
Hrithik, sit. You think your chacha never had his heart broken? When I was twenty, in Bhopal, I was seeing a girl from my college for a year. Nobody at home knew. Then she ended it, and the same week your Dadi found a card from her in my bag.
Oh, the shouting. Your Dada said I had shamed the family by sneaking around. I did the foolish thing first: I lied that it was a friend's card. Then I had to lie about the lie. For two weeks I barely spoke at dinner.
Finally I sat with your Dadi alone in the kitchen. I told her: yes, there was someone, it ended, and I was sad. I didn't tell her every detail; that part was mine. She was quiet, then put extra ghee on my roti. Your Dada took longer.
So I, Samir, your old chacha, am telling you: a breakup is something you learn from, not a disgrace to hide.

qa.q: What did Hrithik's Dadi find in Samir's bag?
qa.a: A card from the girl he had been seeing.

qa.q: How did Samir feel during the two weeks after he lied?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and trapped, barely speaking at dinner, because each lie needed another lie.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Samir's story, and why did it work?
qa.a: Sitting alone with Dadi in the kitchen and telling only what he chose: there was someone, it ended, he was sad. Honesty with limits made room for her compassion.

qa.q: How might Dadi have seen Samir's confession in the kitchen?
qa.a: She seemed to soften, seeing a sad son rather than a disgrace, and showed it by quietly putting extra ghee on his roti.

grounding: Shows parents discovering a relationship and its end, the trap of lying deeper, and choosing what to share so the breakup becomes learning, not disgrace.

passage:
Jasleen's phone was at six percent when Papa called for the third time. The overnight bus to Ludhiana was packed and loud, a film blaring from the screen at the front.
"Your Bua saw photos of you with some boy. And now she says it's over? Were you going to tell us anything?"
Jasleen's first instinct was to say it was a group photo, nothing more. Dolma, her roommate squeezed in beside her, shook her head slightly.
Jasleen took a breath. "Papa, yes, I was with someone for a few months. It ended. I'm sad about it, and I'd rather talk properly at home, not on a bus."
Silence, then: "Are you all right?"
"Not really. But I will be."
The call dropped as the battery died. Jasleen leaned against the window, trembling. Dolma handed her a charger cable and half an orange. "You told the truth you chose. That's enough for tonight."

qa.q: What percentage was Jasleen's phone at when Papa called?
qa.a: Six percent.

qa.q: Why did Jasleen first want to call it a group photo?
qa.a: She felt panicked and ashamed at being judged and wanted to escape Papa's anger with a quick lie.

qa.q: What worked about how Jasleen handled the call?
qa.a: She admitted the relationship and the breakup, said she was sad, and asked to talk properly at home, sharing what she chose instead of lying deeper.

qa.q: How does Papa's tone change during the call?
qa.a: He starts angry about what Bua saw, but after Jasleen's honest answer he asks "Are you all right?", showing worry for her.

grounding: Illustrates family judgement after learning of a relationship and breakup, and choosing honest, limited sharing over lying under pressure.

At Rukmini's mehendi, in the courtyard of her family's house in Nandgaon, Zeenat was balancing a plate of pakoras when she saw Jagdish by the water drum. They hadn't spoken since the rainy season, when things ended badly.
Her first urge was to laugh loudly with the cousins so he'd see how happy she was. Her second was to say something sharp about the girl he'd been seen with at the market.
She did neither. When he came near, she nodded. "Jagdish. How are your parents?"
"Fine. Yours?"
"Good. Amma's knees are better."
A pause. "Nice to see you," he said.
"You too. Enjoy the evening." She turned back to Rukmini, who was holding up hennaed palms to dry.
Her heart was still thudding, but her voice had stayed even. Later, walking home past the dark fields, she felt oddly light.

qa.q: Where did Zeenat see Jagdish?
qa.a: By the water drum at Rukmini's mehendi.

qa.q: What urges did Zeenat feel on seeing Jagdish, and what do they show?
qa.a: She was tempted to laugh loudly to look happy or make a sharp remark, which shows she still felt hurt and wanted to prove something.

qa.q: What made Zeenat's response wise?
qa.a: She was polite, brief and calm, asked after his parents, and went back to Rukmini instead of performing or sniping.

qa.q: How might Jagdish have experienced the short exchange?
qa.a: Probably with relief, since a calm greeting let him say "Nice to see you" without a scene.

Nour saw Paulo the moment she walked into Inês's birthday dinner at a small Lisbon restaurant: he was already seated, and the only free chair was across from him.
"Hi," she said, sitting down. "Nice to see Inês so happy."
"Yeah. Hi."
Through the grilled sardines she noticed herself rehearsing a list, the internship, the trip to Porto, ready to prove she was thriving. She let it go and asked the woman beside her about her pottery class instead.
Over dessert Paulo leaned in. "We should get coffee sometime. Be friends properly."
Nour felt the old pull and set her fork down. "I'm glad we can sit at the same table. I don't think I want coffee, though. Take care, Paulo."
He nodded, a little stung. She helped carry the cake plates to the counter, hugged Inês goodbye at eleven, and walked to the tram with her hands in her coat pockets, breathing out slowly.

passage:
Nilesh, you look the way I did at twenty-one. Sit, drink your tea. I'm Sarita, yes, the boring one from accounts, but listen.
I was with a boy named Prakash for two years in Pune. When it ended, I cried in the ladies' hostel bathroom for weeks. My roommate declared, "That's it, no more love for me either," and she kept that vow for years.
About six months later, I was buying guavas at the market and heard a song we used to love. And I noticed: no stab. Just a small smile. That was the day I sat down and wrote two lists. What was good: he made me laugh, he believed in my exams. What I learned: I kept making myself smaller so he wouldn't be upset. That was my pattern, not only his fault.
I didn't give up on love. I just walked into the next one with my eyes open. You will too.

qa.q: Where was Sarita when she noticed the song no longer hurt?
qa.a: Buying guavas at the market.

qa.q: What did Sarita feel when she heard the old song six months later?
qa.a: Calm and a little warm: no stab of pain, just a small smile, a sign she had healed.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Sarita's story, and what did she do with it?
qa.a: Noticing the song didn't hurt; she then wrote two lists, the good parts and her own habit of making herself smaller, instead of calling the whole relationship bad.

qa.q: How did Sarita's roommate respond to heartbreak differently?
qa.a: She swore off love for years, protecting herself instead of learning, while Sarita kept her heart open with clearer eyes.

grounding: Shows reaching a point where an ex no longer hurts and drawing balanced lessons about one's own patterns, rather than swearing off love.

passage:
The 6:15 local was cancelled because of flooding at Kurla, and Aadhya and Salma were stuck on a crowded platform bench with one umbrella between them.
Salma scrolled past a photo and froze. "Isn't that Vivek? Engaged?"
Aadhya looked. Eight months ago that would have wrecked her evening. Now she felt only a small, surprised quiet. "Good for him. Really."
"You're not upset?"
"Not really. He was kind to my Nani when she was in hospital. He also never once asked what I wanted to study. Both are true."
Salma, still raw from her own breakup in March, pulled her dupatta tight. "I'm never doing this again. Love is a trap."
Aadhya bumped her shoulder. "I said that too. What helped was noticing what I kept ignoring, like needing someone curious about my life. Not quitting."
The announcement crackled: next train in forty minutes. They shared the umbrella and a packet of peanuts, and waited.

qa.q: Why was the 6:15 local cancelled?
qa.a: Because of flooding at Kurla.

qa.q: What did Aadhya feel on seeing Vivek's engagement photo?
qa.a: Only a small, surprised quiet instead of hurt, showing she had moved past the pain in eight months.

qa.q: What would you advise Salma, based on what Aadhya shares?
qa.a: To notice what she needs from a partner and what she kept ignoring, rather than swearing off love while the hurt is fresh.

qa.q: How does Salma see love right now?
qa.a: As a trap to avoid forever; she is still raw from her breakup in March, so Aadhya's calm surprises her.

grounding: Illustrates thinking of an ex months later without hurt, holding both good and bad memories, and learning about one's needs instead of swearing off love.

Workshop facilitator's notes, second-year session, Friday
During the "what does a yes look like" activity, Anand asked to share something. He said that last weekend, walking Deepika back to her hostel, he had wanted to kiss her and leaned in. She went still and looked at the gate. He stopped and asked, "Is this okay?" She said, "Maybe not today." He told the group he had felt embarrassed, then relieved that he had asked.
A few students laughed nervously. One said, "She'd have been fine with it." Anand shook his head. "Her going quiet wasn't a yes. And she can change her mind later, either way."
The room went serious. I used his example to move into our next activity on reading hesitation, and afterwards thanked him privately for his honesty. I have also added a short slide on consent that can change, for next week's batch.

qa.q: What did Deepika say when Anand asked, "Is this okay?"
qa.a: "Maybe not today."

qa.q: How did Anand feel after stopping to ask Deepika?
qa.a: Embarrassed at first, then relieved that he had asked instead of assuming.

qa.q: How did the facilitator use Anand's story?
qa.a: To lead into an activity on reading hesitation, then thanked him privately and added a slide on consent that can change for the next batch.

qa.q: How might Deepika have felt when Anand stopped and asked?
qa.a: Respected and safe: her quiet signal was noticed, and she could say "not today" without pressure.

grounding: Shows wanting closeness and choosing to ask and listen, treating hesitation or silence as not a yes.

passage:
Diary, 14 Nov, late
Movie night in Vasudha's room. Halfway through I really wanted to cuddle up. Old me would've just leaned in and seen what happened. Instead I asked, "Can I sit closer?" Vasudha grinned and said yes, so I did, and it was lovely.
Then during the second film she shifted and went a bit quiet. I didn't want to make it weird, but I asked anyway: "Still good?" She said, "Actually, I'm tired, can we just sit normally?"
For one second I felt a sting. Did I do something wrong? But no. A yes an hour ago isn't a yes forever. I moved back, grabbed my own pillow, and we finished the film laughing at the terrible dubbing.
Walking back to my hostel I felt weirdly proud. Asking felt awkward the first time and easy the second. Note to self: keep asking.
— Minakshi

qa.q: What did Vasudha say when asked "Still good?"
qa.a: "Actually, I'm tired, can we just sit normally?"

qa.q: What did Minakshi feel when Vasudha asked to sit normally?
qa.a: A quick sting of worry about having done something wrong, then calm acceptance that an earlier yes isn't a yes forever.

qa.q: What habit is Minakshi building, and why does it matter?
qa.a: Asking out loud and checking again when things change; it keeps closeness wanted by both, and it gets easier with practice.

qa.q: How might Vasudha see Minakshi's "Still good?"
qa.a: As a caring check that made it easy to say she was tired, without awkwardness or guilt.

grounding: Illustrates asking before closeness and listening when a yes changes, since consent can shift during the same evening.
